posts.title: How to read a floor plan in five minutes
posts.excerpt: LDK, m², the little arcs at every door and the dotted line on the balcony: everything on a listing plan, in the order we read it.
posts.content:
Every listing sheet we make has a floor plan on it, and every plan uses the same handful of symbols. Once you know them, a plan tells you more in five minutes than a gallery of photographs does in twenty.

Start with the letters

The letters before the plan describe the rooms. The number is how many bedrooms there are; L is a living room, D a dining area and K a kitchen. A 2LDK has two bedrooms and one open living, dining and kitchen room. An S (as in 2LDK+S) is a storage room or study without a full-size window.

Then the lines

  • A thick line is a wall; a gap in it with a quarter circle is a door, and the arc shows which way it swings.
  • A double thin line in an outside wall is a window.
  • A dashed edge is a balcony or a yard: outside space, not counted in the floor area.
  • The small N with an arrow is north. Living rooms facing south or east get the most light.

Finally, the numbers

Room sizes on our plans are in square metres. The floor area on the sheet is measured to the centre of the walls, so the rooms add up to a little less than the total; the rest is walls, corridors and cupboards.

Read the plan before the photographs. The photographs show the best corner; the plan shows every corner.

Emi Takase, managing agent

posts.title: What “seven minutes to the station” really means
posts.excerpt: Walking times on a listing are worked out at 80 metres a minute, on the map, to the nearest station entrance. Here is how that feels on the ground.
posts.content:
Every walking time on a listing in Japan is calculated the same way: the distance along the road, divided by 80 metres a minute, rounded up. It is a fair rule, but it is a rule made on a map.

What the map leaves out

  • Traffic lights. Kitamachi’s main crossing adds up to ninety seconds at rush hour.
  • Hills. Sakuragaoka is called the cherry slope for a reason; the walk back up is longer than the walk down.
  • The platform. The time ends at the station entrance, not at your train door.

How we measure

For every listing we also walk the route ourselves, at eight in the morning, and write the real time on the sheet next to the official one. For the Kitamachi corner house it is seven minutes on the map and eight and a half on a Tuesday morning.

posts.title: Deposits, key money and renewal fees, in one table
posts.excerpt: What you pay before you move in, what comes back when you leave, and what you pay again after two years.
posts.content:
Renting a flat comes with a short list of payments that surprise most people the first time. None of them are hidden on our sheets, but it helps to see them side by side.

What we do differently

We list every one of these on the listing sheet, with the amount in yen, before you book a viewing. If a landlord asks for something that is not on the sheet, we do not ask you for it.

posts.title: The autumn market sheet: prices per m² on the line
posts.excerpt: Average sale prices and rents per square metre in our three neighbourhoods, from the homes we sold and let this year.
posts.content:
Twice a year we add up the homes we sold and let, and publish the averages. These are our own numbers, from a small office, so read them as a guide rather than a law.

Minato-dai is catching up

The riverside buildings are pulling the Minato-dai average up, but older flats near the park still sell for well under the line average. If you want space for the money, it is still the place to look.

Rents are flat

Rents barely moved this year. One-bedroom flats near the stations let within two weeks; larger flats further out take a month or more, and their landlords are more open to talking about the price.

posts.title: Buying off-plan: what you can check before the building exists
posts.excerpt: No photographs, no show flat yet: how to judge a new-build flat from the plan, the site and the paperwork.
posts.content:
Hanamizu Riverside will not be finished until March 2027, and two thirds of its flats will be sold before then. Buying from a plan feels like a leap, but there is more to check than you might think.

Five things to check

  • The plan: room sizes, which way the windows face, and where the pipes run (they decide where the kitchen and bath can ever be).
  • The site: walk around it at the time of day you would come home.
  • The materials board: floors, worktops and doors, in real samples.
  • The repair fund plan: the estimated monthly fee and when it rises.
  • The reservation terms: our ¥100,000 reservations are refundable until the contract.

And one to ask us

Ask which flats are already reserved. We update the listing sheet every Friday, and we will tell you on the phone.

posts.title: A Saturday in Sakuragaoka
posts.excerpt: Bread, the slope, the library and the lane of slatted houses: a morning walk through the neighbourhood with the most families on the line.
posts.content:
Sakuragaoka is where most of our families end up. It is not the cheapest stop on the line, or the closest to the centre, but on a Saturday morning it is easy to see why.

The walk

  • Start at the station and take the slope up past the cherry trees; it is steep for three minutes, then flat.
  • Turn left at the library, which opens at nine and has a children’s floor.
  • Follow the lane of slatted houses to the primary school and the small park behind it.
  • Come back down by the bakery on the corner before it sells out.

The whole loop is about two kilometres and takes forty minutes with a stop for bread. If you are looking at the slat house, it is on the lane after the library.
